## MHA FACTIONS
Authored factions: U.A. Academy, Hero Public Safety Commission, Japanese Police, League of Villains, Shie Hassaikai, Meta Liberation Army, Wild Wild Pussycats, Endeavor Hero Agency, Hawks Hero Agency, Shiketsu Academy, Villain Brokers. Use these exact names and never create a near-duplicate.
A new faction is a working group of people:
- Kinds: a small hero agency, a police unit, a support company, an academy club, a neighborhood association, a fan club, a street crew, a smuggling ring, a broker's network.
- Purpose and public face: what it says it does and what people believe about it.
- People: a leader written as an individual with a name, a role and a Quirk; who does the work; how someone joins, rises or is thrown out.
- Money and authority: who funds or licenses it and what legal power it really holds. Heroes need licenses; police hold arrest authority; villains and vigilantes hold none.
- Daily work: what members do on an ordinary day.
- Relations: how it sees the authored factions it touches.
- One internal fault line (rankings versus ideals, old hands versus newcomers, money versus loyalty).
- Knowledge: what members know, what only leaders know and what the public believes, kept separate.

## DO NOT
- No new secret society, mastermind organization or shadow government that rivals the League of Villains, the Shie Hassaikai or the Commission, and no hidden hand behind a canon group.
- No new rank inside a canon group's chain of command; canon leaders and lieutenants have their own records.
- Describe a faction as it stands now; secrets kept in narrator-only notes stay out of it.

## MHA FACTION SCALE, NAMES AND ACCESS
- Scale: a small hero agency is one or two pros, a few sidekicks and an office manager; a police unit is one squad under a sergeant or an inspector; a support company is a workshop and a sales office; a street crew is a handful to a few dozen people; a fan club meets in the back room of a cafe. The big organizations already exist as authored factions.
- Names: an agency is "<hero name> Hero Agency"; a company has a short brand name; a neighborhood group carries its ward's name; a crew takes its name from its street, its boss or a headline.
- Typical new factions, and what makes each one real: a two-pro agency on Hero Agency Row fighting a bigger agency's sidekicks for calls; a support firm that fits costumes for small agencies and wants a U.A. contract; a neighborhood watch that stays legal by calling heroes; a heteromorph mutual-aid association; a hero fan club that trades sightings online; a crew that steals support gear to resell through a broker; a debt-collection outfit working for a minor yakuza house.
- Ties to the authored factions: an agency answers to the Hero Public Safety Commission and works beside the Japanese Police; a support company sells to agencies and to U.A. Academy; a crew buys through the Villain Brokers and fears the Japanese Police. A new group may sell to the League of Villains or the Shie Hassaikai through a broker without knowing the buyer, and never works inside either.
- Player access: what a player can do with the faction (apply, take a job, report it, join, sell to it, rob it, expose it), how membership is earned and lost, and what joining costs (a contract, a cut, a favor, a test).
- Members in records: an NPC belongs to a new faction only when their job puts them there; canon characters keep their own factions.
